<reason>Both sides were strong, but PRO built the cleaner path to victory. PRO's opening framed a memorable moral core (sellers paid in full reclaiming the goods), dismantled CON's gym/lease analogy by distinguishing one-time payment from ongoing service, and defused the resale-collapse argument by showing death is involuntary, unrepeatable, and non-substitutive for new sales. CON landed real hits — the perpetual generational chain, retroactive rewriting of settled contracts, the "next of kin" drafting flaw that overrides wills, and the subscription-flight scenario — but two of CON's five turns were clipped, and the closing concession ("it's the friction, not the principle") handed PRO a decisive turn: "death is the friction." CON's "certain cost, possibly empty promise" closing frame was sharp, yet PRO had already qualified it with the plausible buy/rent bifurcation and the tension that CON cannot call honest pricing catastrophic while defending the current arrangement as honest. PRO answered both pressure questions directly and kept the daughter-with-900-ebooks remedy pressure alive; CON's consumer-law answer genuinely addressed the buyer but never fully delivered anything to the heir. PRO wins a competitive but clear debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The chain-of-transfers clash: CON argued "one estate, one transfer" dissolves into an infinite willable chain [B2.2]; PRO countered that death is involuntary and non-substitutive [A2.3]; CON's friction answer [B4.1-B4.2] conceded inheritance is fine "in principle," which PRO converted into the decisive "death is the friction" close [A5.1-A5.2].</best_rebuttal>
